title: Isaac of Mosul

full_text:
Isaac of Mosul was the chief court musician of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, universally acknowledged as the greatest master of the lute and the voice in all the Islamic world. His melodies moved emperors to tears and his compositions were sung from Cordoba to Baghdad.

One sultry afternoon, desiring to escape the formalities of the court, Isaac walked through the quiet residential quarters of Baghdad. Passing a secluded garden enclosed by high walls, his ear was caught by the sound of a lute being played with such breathtaking subtlety, technical perfection, and soulful depth that Isaac stood frozen on the cobblestones.

A youthful voice sang verses of heartbreaking beauty, modulating across complex melodic modes with effortless grace. Isaac listened, his heart alternating between awe and astonishment. He realized that this unknown lutenist possessed a genius that rivaled—and perhaps surpassed—his own.

Instead of turning away in envious bitterness, Isaac knocked upon the gate. A modest young man named Ziryab, poorly dressed but with eyes burning with artistic devotion, opened the door.

Isaac smiled warmly, embraced the youth, and said: 'Young master, I am Isaac of Mosul. I have spent my life mastering the lute, yet your playing has opened a new fountain of wonder in my soul. You must not hide your light in a courtyard; the world must hear your song!'

Isaac brought Ziryab to the palace, presented him to the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, and stepped back to let the young artist perform before the court. The Caliph was enchanted, rewarding Ziryab with wealth and honor. Years later, Ziryab traveled to Andalusia, where he founded the legendary conservatory of Cordoba, revolutionizing music and poetry across Europe.

Isaac’s generosity was celebrated as a rare example of true greatness: a master who nurtured his own rival, proving that art belongs not to the ego, but to the beauty of all humankind.
moral: A true master of art recognizes and honors talent in others without the poison of petty jealousy.
